newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Exhausted nurses want to leave volcano-hit Montserrat.
newsitem.headline: Exhausted nurses want to leave volcano-hit Montserrat.

text.p: Nurses on volcano-hit Montserrat want to leave, saying they are exhausted by the relief effort and fear for their own safety since the Soufriere Hills volcano flared again two weeks ago.
They have complained about poor work conditions at the makeshift hospital in St. John's and a lack of medical supplies on the Caribbean island, a tiny British colony.

At least 22 people were listed as dead or missing as a result of huge flows of superheated rock, gases and ash from the volcano on June 25. Rock flows wiped out seven villages and several hundred people have left the island since then.
Chief Minister Bertrand Osborne met on Friday with about 35 nurses who wanted to leave in a bid to allay their fears.

But Charmaine Thompson, head of the Trained Nurses and Mid-wife Association, said on Tuesday: "There are a number of nurses who still think that they need a break because they feel that they are burned out and they have reached a point where if they were to continue for any length of time they would break."
About 60 nurses work at the makeshift hospital in St. John's, which was opened after the capital Plymouth was abandoned in 1995 becuase its proximity to the volcano.
Thompson said conditions at the hospital were atrocious. Many of the nurses had been forced to abandon homes in unsafe zones themselves, she said.
Six nurses from Jamaica have arrived to help and other Caribbean neighbours have pledged to send teams.

The volcanic activity is the worst since Soufriere Hills roared to life in July, 1995, after nearly four centuries of dormancy. As many as 700 people had left since the latest activity, leaving about 5,800 people on the island, in the eastern Caribbean 25 miles (40 km) southwest of Antigua. The population was about 11,000 before the volcano came alive.
